newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lines drawn in spat over German DePfa stake.
newsitem.headline: Lines drawn in spat over German DePfa stake.

text.p: Confusion reigned on Tuesday as German mortgage lender DePfa-Bank AG stuck by an allegation that UBS had bought nine percent of its shares despite a categorical denial by the Swiss banking giant.

DePfa's shares, which soared after it made its charge, remaining strong even after UBS's denial as the second-tier German bank emerged as a hot new potential takeover candidate in a market which has been rife with merger talk for months.
The episode divided analysts. A sceptical Paribas Bank opted to downgrade DePfa to a "sell" after the news while Merck, Finck raised the bank to a "buy".

The commotion began when DePfa issued a statement early on Tuesday, saying it believed that UBS, long rumoured to be interested in the German market, had built up a substantial stake in its capital on the open market.
DePfa's shares surged as much as 13 percent to an all-time high of 91 marks as speculation mounted that UBS may be seeking a controlling stake in the bank.
But Union Bank of Switzerland flatly denied the statement and insisted its stake in DePfa was below one percent. It also said a takeover of DePfa would not at all fit its strategy.
Nonetheless, DePfa remained a focus of market attention, slipping slightly to 89 marks for a gain of 10 percent on a day when the broad market advanced less than one percent.
UBS shares were largely unaffected by the DePfa story, traders said. UBS bearer shares closed seven Swiss francs higher at 1,355 francs, in line with Swiss financial stocks.
Some analysts said a takeover of DePfa would make sense for UBS, which may need a stronger presence in the euro zone as the start of monetary union looms.

Konrad Becker, banking analyst at Merck, Finck in Duesseldorf, said: "I don't know if UBS will launch a takeover bid but I could imagine it. DePfa has now been put on the map as a takeover candidate, it wasn't regarded as one before."

Under a new chief executive since last year, UBS has set its sights on expanding in asset management -- a field in which DePfa is not active -- while trimming more costly businesses, chiefly retail banking and corporate lending.

Chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta last month said part of this strategy was likely to include acquisitions but limited the scope of interest to asset management and private banking operations, especially in the U.S.

DePfa itself said talk of a takeover bid would be "pure speculation" but a spokesman added that the bank, as a leading leading provider of state financing across Europe, may be interesting for a Swiss bank preparing for monetary union.
Late on Tuesday the bank repeated its conviction that UBS had bought its stock.

"We continue to affirm that UBS holds nine percent. Whether the stake is held in its asset management division or somewhere else, we don't know," a spokesman said. The shares, he said, were being held in Zurich and London.
UBS equally stuck to its guns, saying it had nothing to add to its early denial.

Germany's biggest issuer of Pfandbrief bonds (used to refinance mortgages or public projects), DePfa has a market capitalisation of about three billion marks ($1.8 billion) and total assets of about 165 billion marks.
Some 60 percent of its capital is widely distributed while the remaining 40 percent is owned by a holding company, DePfa-Holding Verwaltungsgesellschaft mbH.

Analysts said the confusion may stem from an 8.2 percent stake in DePfa held by Swiss insurer Swiss Life. UBS will own 25 percent of Swiss Life if the insurer gains approval for a planned conversion into a listed company on June 30.
DePfa rejected this theory, a spokesman saying: "There will have to be some talks at board level." ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
